analogy.p: Imagine a town's water system with a single pump house that sends water first out to a nearby filtration plant (the lungs) and, once it returns, pumps it again at high pressure out to every house in town (the body): the same pump is used twice for each lap, which is the double circulation. The big pipes leaving the pump are thick-walled arteries, the returning pipes are thin-walled veins with one-way gates (valves), and the tiny pipes at each house are capillaries where the water is handed over. The analogy breaks down because a real heart is a living muscle that needs its own blood supply, blood is a tissue with cells and not just fluid, and the blood is returned and reused rather than being used up.
analogy.t: A two-lap relay with one pump house

bullets: The **heart** is an organ that pumps blood around the body in a **double circulatory system**.
You must name: **right and left atrium, right and left ventricle, vena cava, pulmonary artery, pulmonary vein, aorta, valves and coronary arteries**.
You must describe **arteries, veins and capillaries** and explain how each is adapted to its function.
You must describe **blood**: **plasma, red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets**, and the function of each.
You must know that **natural pacemaker cells** in the right atrium control the resting heart rate, and that **artificial pacemakers** correct irregularities.
Maths skills: rate of blood flow as volume divided by time, reading data from tables and graphs, and magnification of cells.
Links: gas exchange in lungs, respiration (cells need oxygen and glucose), the immune system, and coronary heart disease (next spec point).
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: AQA 8461 (4.2.2.1 to 4.2.2.3) asks you to describe how the **heart**, **blood vessels** and **blood** work together as the body's **transport system**. You must know that the human circulatory system is a **double circulatory system**, be able to name and locate the four chambers of the heart and the main vessels, and explain how the structure of each part (muscular walls, valves, wall thickness, lumen size) is related to its function. You must also know the components of blood and the job of each. Typical questions ask you to label a heart diagram, trace the path of blood, explain why arteries and veins differ, or explain how red blood cells are adapted.

bullets: The circulatory system moves blood to **all cells** quickly, much faster than diffusion alone.
Cells need **oxygen and glucose** for **aerobic respiration**, which releases energy.
**Carbon dioxide** and **urea** are waste products that must be removed.
Blood is pumped by the **heart**, carried in **blood vessels**, and the cells and fluid inside are the **blood**.
The circulatory system links with the **breathing system** (oxygen in, carbon dioxide out) and the **digestive system** (food in).
Cells in a very small organism get what they need by diffusion alone, so they need no circulatory system.
Link: the heart, vessels and blood together form an **organ system**; the heart is an organ made of muscle, glandular and connective tissue.
core.h: Why a multicellular organism needs a transport system
core.p: Large animals have a **small surface area to volume ratio**, so diffusion across the body surface is far too slow to supply cells deep in the body. They need an **exchange surface** (the lungs) to take in oxygen and a **transport system** (the blood, pumped by the heart) to carry substances between the exchange surfaces and every cell. Blood carries **oxygen** to respiring cells, **dissolved digested food (glucose and amino acids)** from the small intestine, **carbon dioxide** to the lungs, **urea** to the kidneys, and **hormones** from glands to target organs. Without a circulation, cells far from the lungs and gut would quickly run out of oxygen and nutrients and be poisoned by their own waste.

bullets: **Loop 1 (pulmonary circulation)**: right ventricle, pulmonary artery, lungs, pulmonary vein, left atrium.
**Loop 2 (systemic circulation)**: left ventricle, aorta, body organs, vena cava, right atrium.
Blood goes through the heart **twice** in each circuit, hence 'double'.
The **right side** of the heart carries **deoxygenated** blood; the **left side** carries **oxygenated** blood.
Pressure is lower in the lungs (delicate capillaries) and higher in the body, so the heart gives the blood a second 'push'.
Fish have a single circulation; mammals and birds have double circulation, which supports a high metabolic rate.
Remember: arteries carry blood **away** from the heart; veins carry blood **to** the heart.
Exceptions to 'arteries carry oxygenated blood': the **pulmonary artery** carries deoxygenated blood, the **pulmonary vein** carries oxygenated blood.
core.p: Humans have a **double circulatory system**, meaning blood passes through the heart **twice** on each complete circuit of the body. In the first loop the **right ventricle** pumps **deoxygenated blood to the lungs** through the **pulmonary artery**, where it picks up oxygen and loses carbon dioxide. This blood returns in the **pulmonary vein** to the left side of the heart. In the second loop the **left ventricle** pumps **oxygenated blood around the body** through the **aorta**, and it returns to the right side of the heart through the **vena cava**. The advantage is that blood returning from the lungs is pumped again at **high pressure** to reach all body cells, which would not happen in a single loop where pressure would be lost in the lungs' small capillaries.

bullets: **Right atrium**: receives deoxygenated blood from the body through the **vena cava**.
**Right ventricle**: pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs through the **pulmonary artery**.
**Left atrium**: receives oxygenated blood from the lungs through the **pulmonary vein**.
**Left ventricle**: pumps oxygenated blood to the body through the **aorta**; it has a **much thicker muscular wall** because it must pump blood at high pressure all around the body.
The **right ventricle** wall is thinner because it only pumps blood to the nearby lungs at lower pressure.
**Atria have thin walls** because they only push blood a short distance into the ventricles.
**Valves** between atria and ventricles, and in the arteries leaving the heart, stop blood flowing backwards.
**Coronary arteries** supply the heart muscle with oxygen and glucose; blockage causes a heart attack (see coronary heart disease).
core.h: Structure of the heart: chambers and vessels
core.p: The heart is a **muscular organ** with **four chambers**. The two upper chambers are the **atria** (singular **atrium**), which receive blood, and the two lower chambers are the **ventricles**, which pump blood out. A wall of muscle called the **septum** separates the right side from the left so oxygenated and deoxygenated blood do not mix. The blood vessels attached to the heart are the **vena cava** (into the right atrium), the **pulmonary artery** (out of the right ventricle), the **pulmonary vein** (into the left atrium) and the **aorta** (out of the left ventricle). The heart muscle itself has its own blood supply, the **coronary arteries**, which branch from the aorta and wrap over the heart.

bullets: **1**. Deoxygenated blood from the body enters the **right atrium** through the **vena cava**.
**2**. The right atrium contracts; blood passes through a **valve** into the **right ventricle**.
**3**. The right ventricle contracts; blood leaves through the **pulmonary artery** to the **lungs**.
**4**. In the lungs blood picks up **oxygen** and loses **carbon dioxide** (gas exchange in the alveoli).
**5**. Oxygenated blood returns through the **pulmonary vein** to the **left atrium**.
**6**. The left atrium contracts; blood passes through a valve into the **left ventricle**.
**7**. The left ventricle contracts strongly; blood leaves through the **aorta** and travels to the body.
**8**. Valves close behind the blood each time, so it **cannot flow backwards**.
core.h: How blood flows through the heart (step by step)
core.p: You should be able to trace the path of blood through the heart and lungs in order. Blood flows in one direction only because valves close when the pressure behind them drops. The atria contract first and push blood into the ventricles, then the ventricles contract and force blood out into the arteries. The sequence below is the one to learn for the exam.

bullets: Valves prevent **backflow** and keep blood moving in the right direction.
The **natural pacemaker** is a group of cells in the **right atrium** that controls the resting heart rate.
An **artificial pacemaker** is an electrical device that corrects irregularities in the heart rate.
During exercise, heart rate rises (controlled by nerves and the hormone adrenaline) so more oxygen reaches muscles.
Heart muscle needs a good supply of oxygen, delivered by the **coronary arteries**.
Faulty heart valves (stiff or leaky) can be replaced with **biological** (from animals) or **mechanical** valves, which makes the heart work more efficiently.
**Mechanical** valves last longer but need anticoagulant drugs; **biological** valves wear out sooner.
core.h: Valves, the pacemaker and heart rate
core.p: **Valves** are flaps of tissue that open to let blood through in one direction and close to stop it flowing back. Without working valves, blood would flow backwards and the heart would pump much less effectively. The heart beats without conscious control because a group of cells in the **right atrium wall**, the **natural pacemaker**, produces regular electrical signals that make the heart muscle contract. This sets the **resting heart rate**. If the natural pacemaker does not work properly, an **artificial pacemaker** can be implanted: a small electrical device that sends regular signals to the heart to keep it beating at the correct rate.

bullets: Carry blood **away from the heart** at **high pressure**.
**Thick walls** withstand the pressure and stop the artery bursting.
**Muscle** in the wall can contract to **control the diameter** and so the flow to organs.
**Elastic fibres** stretch and recoil, evening out the pulse.
**Narrow lumen** helps maintain pressure.
No valves (except at the start of the aorta and pulmonary artery, which are heart valves).
The pulse you feel at your wrist or neck is caused by the surge of blood in an artery.
Examples: **aorta**, **pulmonary artery**, **coronary arteries**.
core.p: **Arteries** carry blood **away from the heart** at **high pressure**. The blood pulses along them with each heartbeat. To withstand this pressure, artery walls are **thick** and contain **layers of muscle** and **elastic fibres**. The elastic fibres allow the wall to **stretch** as blood surges through and then **recoil** to help push the blood along. The **lumen** (the hole in the centre) is relatively **narrow**, which helps to keep the pressure high. Arteries carry blood to the body organs and to the lungs.

bullets: Carry blood **to the heart** at **low pressure**.
**Thinner walls**: less pressure to withstand.
**Wide lumen**: reduces resistance to blood flow.
**Valves** prevent backflow, so blood moves in one direction only.
Blood is squeezed along by the **contraction of nearby muscles**.
Examples: **vena cava**, **pulmonary vein**.
Veins are often closer to the surface than arteries, which is why they are used for taking blood samples.
Remember the key link: low pressure means thin walls and valves; high pressure means thick, elastic walls.
core.p: **Veins** carry blood **towards the heart** at **low pressure**. Because the pressure is low, the walls can be **thinner**, with less muscle and elastic tissue. The **lumen is wider**, so blood flows with less resistance. Because the pressure is too low to push the blood back up to the heart (especially from the legs), veins contain **valves** that stop blood flowing backwards. Blood is also pushed along when surrounding **skeletal muscles** squeeze the veins as you move.

bullets: **Walls one cell thick** give a **short diffusion distance** for fast exchange.
**Very narrow** (about the width of a red blood cell), so blood flows slowly and cells are close to the blood.
A **large total surface area** is provided by the huge number of capillaries.
**Permeable walls** allow substances to move out and in.
Oxygen and glucose diffuse **out** of the blood into cells; carbon dioxide and urea diffuse **in**.
Capillaries have no valves and thin walls because the pressure is low by the time blood reaches them.
Link: the same idea (short distance, large area) is seen in the alveoli and villi.
core.p: **Capillaries** are the smallest blood vessels. They form dense networks (capillary beds) around cells and around the alveoli in the lungs and the villi in the gut. Their walls are only **one cell thick**, so the **diffusion distance is very short**, and they are so narrow that blood moves slowly, giving **more time for exchange**. They are permeable, so substances such as **oxygen, glucose and carbon dioxide diffuse** between the blood and the cells. They link **arteries to veins**.

bullets: **Direction**: arteries away from the heart; veins to the heart; capillaries between arteries and veins.
**Wall**: artery thick (muscle and elastic); vein thin; capillary one cell thick.
**Lumen**: artery narrow; vein wide; capillary very narrow.
**Pressure**: artery high; vein low; capillary low and falling.
**Valves**: only in veins.
**Function**: arteries carry blood at high pressure around the body; veins return blood; capillaries allow exchange.
**Example**: aorta / vena cava / capillary beds in muscle.
Remember cross-section pictures: the artery has a thick ring of wall and a small hole; the vein has a larger hole and thin wall.
core.p: Comparison questions are common and you should answer them with a structured approach: wall, lumen, pressure, direction, valves and example. A table is a good way to revise it, and you can reproduce it in prose in the exam using words like 'whereas'. Always link the structure to the function, not just describe it.

bullets: Plasma is the **liquid part** of blood; it is mostly water.
It carries **dissolved** substances: **glucose, amino acids, carbon dioxide, urea, hormones, proteins and mineral ions**.
It distributes **heat** from active organs such as muscles and liver around the body.
The cells and platelets are suspended in the plasma.
Plasma is straw coloured; **red blood cells** make blood red.
Digested food enters the plasma in the capillaries of the **small intestine villi**.
**Carbon dioxide** is carried mainly dissolved in plasma.
Blood volume is about 5 litres in an adult (use if given data).
core.p: **Blood** is a tissue made of **plasma** with **red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets** suspended in it. **Plasma** is a pale yellow, watery liquid that makes up just over half of the blood. It **transports** many dissolved substances around the body: **carbon dioxide** (from organs to the lungs), **digested food** such as **glucose and amino acids** (from the small intestine to cells), **urea** (from the liver to the kidneys), **hormones** (from glands to target organs) and **heat**.

bullets: **Biconcave disc** shape: large surface area for oxygen to diffuse in and out.
**No nucleus**: more space for haemoglobin, so more oxygen carried per cell.
**Haemoglobin** (contains iron): binds reversibly to oxygen, **haemoglobin + oxygen is oxyhaemoglobin**, and releases it where oxygen concentration is low.
**Flexible and small**: can pass through capillaries in single file.
Red blood cells are made in the **bone marrow**.
Reaction: **haemoglobin + oxygen ⇌ oxyhaemoglobin** (forward in the lungs, backward in the tissues).
Red blood cells **do not carry** carbon dioxide in the AQA GCSE content; plasma does.
Lack of red cells or haemoglobin causes **anaemia**: tiredness and shortness of breath.
core.p: **Red blood cells** carry **oxygen** from the lungs to all the body cells. They are packed with a red protein called **haemoglobin**, which binds with oxygen in the lungs to form **oxyhaemoglobin** and releases it in the body tissues. Their structure is adapted to this job: they are a **biconcave disc** (dimpled on both sides), giving a **large surface area to volume ratio** for absorbing oxygen quickly; they have **no nucleus**, leaving more room for haemoglobin; and they are small and flexible so they can squeeze through narrow capillaries.

bullets: **Phagocytes**: engulf pathogens and digest them (phagocytosis); they can change shape.
**Lymphocytes**: produce **antibodies** against specific pathogens; also produce **antitoxins**.
White cells have a **nucleus**; this is a key way to tell them from red cells.
**Platelets**: cell fragments that **help blood to clot** at a wound.
A scab forms from the clot, **sealing the wound** and keeping microbes out.
Lack of platelets or clotting factors leads to **excessive bleeding**; too much clotting inside vessels can cause thrombosis.
Link: these cells are covered in more depth under **the immune system and vaccination**.
The exam command 'describe how white blood cells protect against disease' needs both phagocytosis and antibodies.
core.h: Blood: white blood cells and platelets
core.p: **White blood cells** are part of the **immune system** and protect the body from **pathogens**. They have a **nucleus**. Two main types: **phagocytes** engulf and digest pathogens (**phagocytosis**), and **lymphocytes** produce **antibodies** that bind to pathogens and **antitoxins** that neutralise toxins. **Platelets** are **small fragments of cells** with **no nucleus**. They help the blood to **clot** at a wound, forming a scab that stops blood loss and prevents microorganisms entering.

bullets: **Rate of blood flow (cm³/min) = volume of blood ÷ time**; e.g. 300 cm³ in 4 minutes is 75 cm³/min.
**Heart rate** is the number of beats per minute; **stroke volume** is the volume pumped per beat (extension: cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume).
**Magnification = image size ÷ real size**; red blood cells are about **7 to 8 µm** across.
**Exchange**: surface area to volume ratio explains the biconcave shape.
**Respiration**: oxygen and glucose delivered by blood are used in mitochondria to release energy.
**Exercise**: heart and breathing rates rise to increase oxygen delivery and carbon dioxide removal.
**Diseases**: narrowing of the coronary arteries (coronary heart disease) reduces blood supply to heart muscle; stents and statins are covered in the next spec point.
**Evaluate** questions on artificial hearts or valves: compare reliability, risk of rejection, cost and need for drugs.
core.p: Many questions on this topic include data. You may have to calculate the **rate of blood flow**, interpret a graph of heart rate, or compare the sizes of cells using magnification. Always show your working and give units. Knowing the basics and the links to other topics also helps with unfamiliar contexts, such as a patient who has a narrowed artery or a cardiac patient with a pacemaker.

exam: **Label the heart (4 to 6 marks)**: use exact names: right atrium, vena cava, pulmonary artery, aorta, pulmonary vein, left ventricle; remember the diagram is viewed from the front.

**Trace the blood flow (4 marks)**: vena cava, right atrium, right ventricle, pulmonary artery, lungs, pulmonary vein, left atrium, left ventricle, aorta; mention valves and that blood goes through the heart twice.
**Why is the left ventricle wall thicker? (2 marks)**: it pumps blood at higher pressure (1) around the whole body, whereas the right ventricle pumps to the nearby lungs (1).
**Compare arteries and veins (3 to 4 marks)**: use comparative words; wall thickness, lumen, pressure, valves, with a function for each.
**Explain how a capillary is adapted (2 to 3 marks)**: wall one cell thick (1) so short diffusion distance (1); narrow so blood flows slowly allowing time for exchange.
**Adaptations of the red blood cell (3 marks)**: biconcave disc gives large surface area; no nucleus so more haemoglobin; haemoglobin binds oxygen.
**Pacemaker questions (2 marks)**: natural pacemaker in the right atrium controls resting heart rate; artificial pacemaker corrects irregularities.
**Calculations**: rate of flow = volume / time with units; magnification = image / real size.
**Double circulation (2 marks)**: blood passes through the heart twice per circuit; lungs first, then body, so blood stays at high pressure.
**Command words**: Name/State = short; Describe = what; Explain = because; Compare = both sides, with 'whereas'.
**Avoid vague terms** such as 'strong' for walls: say 'thick and muscular' or 'elastic'; and 'carries oxygen' needs 'haemoglobin'.

mistakes.r: Arteries carry blood away from the heart and veins towards it; the pulmonary artery is deoxygenated and the pulmonary vein is oxygenated.
mistakes.w: Arteries carry oxygenated blood and veins carry deoxygenated blood.

mistakes.r: The left ventricle has a thicker muscle wall because it pumps blood at high pressure around the whole body.
mistakes.w: The left ventricle is thicker because it is bigger.

mistakes.r: Valves prevent backflow; they close to stop blood flowing the wrong way.
mistakes.w: Blood flows backwards if the valves are open.

mistakes.r: Red blood cells have no nucleus, giving more room for haemoglobin.
mistakes.w: Red blood cells have a nucleus so they can carry more.

mistakes.r: Veins have thin walls because pressure is low; they have valves and a wide lumen.
mistakes.w: Veins have thick walls because blood is under pressure.

mistakes.r: Capillary walls are one cell thick, giving a short diffusion distance; blood flows slowly so there is time for exchange.
mistakes.w: Capillaries have thin walls so blood flows through quickly.

mistakes.r: Blood passes through the heart twice per circuit: it is a double circulatory system.
mistakes.w: The heart pumps blood once around the body (single circulation).

mistakes.r: Coronary arteries supply the heart muscle with oxygen and glucose.
Red blood cells carry oxygen; white blood cells defend against pathogens.
Diagrams show the heart from the front, so the heart's right side is on the left of the page.
mistakes.w: The right side of the heart is on the right of the diagram.

summary: AQA expects you to describe the human double circulatory system, name the chambers and vessels of the heart and the path of blood through them, explain how arteries, veins and capillaries are adapted to their functions, and describe plasma, red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets. It matters because transport underpins gas exchange, respiration, immunity and heart disease.

terms.d: A circulatory system in which blood passes through the heart twice on each complete circuit of the body.
An upper chamber of the heart that receives blood.
A lower chamber of the heart that pumps blood out.
The vein that carries deoxygenated blood from the body to the right atrium.
The artery that carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs.
The vein that carries oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium.
The artery that carries oxygenated blood from the left ventricle to the body.
A flap of tissue that stops blood flowing backwards.
Arteries that supply the heart muscle with oxygenated blood.
A group of cells in the right atrium that controls the resting heart rate (an artificial one is an electrical device that corrects irregularities).
A blood vessel that carries blood away from the heart at high pressure; it has thick, elastic, muscular walls.
A blood vessel that carries blood towards the heart at low pressure; it has thin walls, a wide lumen and valves.
A very small blood vessel with walls one cell thick, where substances are exchanged with the cells.
The liquid part of blood that carries blood cells and dissolved substances such as glucose, carbon dioxide, urea and hormones.
The red protein in red blood cells that binds oxygen to form oxyhaemoglobin.
Small fragments of cells that help blood to clot.
A white blood cell that engulfs and digests pathogens.
A white blood cell that produces antibodies and antitoxins.

worked.ans: Model answer: Deoxygenated blood enters the right atrium through the vena cava, passes through a valve into the right ventricle, which pumps it through the pulmonary artery to the lungs. Oxygenated blood returns through the pulmonary vein to the left atrium, passes through a valve into the left ventricle and is pumped out through the aorta to the body.
worked.q: Describe the path of blood from the body to the lungs and back to the body, naming the heart chambers and blood vessels in order. (4 marks)
steps: Body to right atrium via the vena cava.
Right atrium to right ventricle through a valve.
Right ventricle to lungs via the pulmonary artery.
Lungs to left atrium via the pulmonary vein, then left ventricle, then out through the aorta.

worked.ans: Arteries have thick, muscular, elastic walls and a narrow lumen to withstand and maintain high pressure, whereas veins have thinner walls and a wide lumen because the pressure is low, and valves to prevent backflow.
worked.q: Explain how the structure of an artery is related to its function, and how a vein differs. (4 marks)
steps: Artery carries blood at high pressure away from the heart, so the wall is thick with muscle and elastic fibres.
The elastic fibres stretch and recoil; the lumen is narrow.
Vein carries blood at low pressure to the heart, so the wall is thinner and the lumen wider.
Veins have valves to stop backflow.
